analysis.one_liner: Bans corporate and union election communications and closes the parties' soft-money loophole.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Administration Committee: it was referred there the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would tighten federal campaign finance rules in two main ways. First, it would treat corporate communications to stockholders and executives, and union communications to members and their families, as restricted election spending rather than as permitted activity, and it would repeal the exemption that let corporations and unions fund nonpartisan voter registration and get-out-the-vote drives; it would also require corporations and unions to disclose any other election-related payments they make. Second, it would ban soft money: political party payments for activities that mix federal election work with other purposes — like general political advertising or voter drives — would have to follow the same limits and reporting rules as regular campaign spending, paid only from federally regulated accounts.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters and candidates running without corporate or union money behind them. By closing the stockholder, member, and soft-money channels, the bill would make it harder for large organizations to bankroll federal election activity outside the normal contribution limits and disclosure rules, which its title describes as making elections more competitive, open, and honest.

how_it_helps.text: Treats corporate communications to stockholders and executive personnel, and union communications to members and their families, as restricted contributions or expenditures when they aim to influence a federal election [S2][S3].
Repeals the provision excluding nonpartisan registration and get-out-the-vote campaigns from the ban, so corporations and unions could no longer fund those drives directly [S2].

Requires corporations and labor organizations to report any other election-related payments to the Federal Election Commission in the same manner as a House or Senate campaign committee reports its spending [S2][S3].

Subjects party payments for 'mixed political activities' — things like voter registration drives, get-out-the-vote efforts, or general political advertising that serve both federal elections and other purposes — to the same limits and reporting as campaign expenditures, paid only from federally regulated accounts, closing the soft-money channel [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, labor unions, and the national and state political parties. Corporations and unions would lose channels they could legally use to communicate with their own stockholders, executives, and members about elections and to fund voter drives; parties would lose the ability to raise and spend unregulated soft money on mixed federal and non-federal activities.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporations, labor unions, and party committees

drawbacks.text: Repealing the nonpartisan voter registration and get-out-the-vote exemption would end a legal funding source for nonpartisan voter outreach, which could reduce voter participation even as it removes a channel for corporate and union influence [S2].

Banning communications even to corporations' own stockholders and executives, and unions' own members and their families, would restrict political speech within organizations to people with a direct stake in them [S2][S3].
The bill would impose new FEC reporting and paperwork requirements on any corporation or union election-related payment, adding compliance costs [S2][S3].
Restricting organized money tends to push spending toward channels the rules do not reach, so the effect on the overall amount of money in federal elections is uncertain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets real loopholes — soft money and the corporate/union communication carve-outs — and would make more federal election money subject to limits and disclosure, which serves voters. The costs are real but modest: some nonpartisan voter outreach funded by unions and corporations would disappear, and compliance burdens would rise. On balance the trade favors transparency and competitive elections, though as a single-line bill from one member it was less comprehensive than broader campaign finance reform proposals.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Administration Committee the day it was introduced, never came out of committee, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Doug Bereuter, a Nebraska Republican, introduced the bill on February 20, 1991 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on House Administration the same day, and no further action was ever taken on it [S5].
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and the bill died without a hearing, a vote, or any movement in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations, labor unions, and the national party committees are better off, because the restrictions on their election communications and soft-money spending never became law.

for.name: Rep. Doug Bereuter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.role: The committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no markup, hearing, or vote was ever recorded, and the bill never reached the House floor.

against.name: Corporations, labor unions, and party committees
against.role: Interests whose election spending the bill would have restricted
against.what_they_did: Held their existing ability to spend on federal elections through corporate/union communications and party soft money, since the bill never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Republican with no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan coalition ever formed around it one way or the other [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would ban corporate communications aimed at influencing federal elections — including messages to stockholders and executives — and would end corporate funding of nonpartisan voter drives, while requiring disclosure of other election-related payments. Corporations currently benefit from these channels, which sit outside normal campaign limits.

The bill would classify union communications to members and their families as restricted election spending and repeal the union exemption for get-out-the-vote campaigns. Unions use these channels today to reach their own members about elections.

industries.industry: National and state political party committees
industries.note: The bill would ban soft money: party spending on mixed federal and non-federal activities like general political advertising and voter drives would have to follow federal contribution limits and reporting, paid from regulated accounts. Parties rely on unregulated soft money for exactly these activities.
